2449274:
This lesson explains how to describe your internal experiences and why those descriptions don't need to make logical sense.

Types of Descriptions: There are many ways to describe sensations: shape, size, location, color, temperature, texture, time, want, action, image, sound, memory, and more. These descriptions are mostly for sensations (not cognitions or emotions).

Whatever Pops Into Your Mind is Right: Descriptions don't need to make sense. Whatever image, word, or feeling pops into your mind is the right answer. Your brain is just trying to relate your internal experience to something, it's providing a reference point.

Example: The Projector Booth: One client described her shutdown state as sitting in a little chair behind a projector, watching the movie of her life play out in front of her eyes. That was her way of describing what it felt like to be in shutdown. This is the kind of description you're aiming for.

Let It Be There: Once you describe the sensation, don't try to make it go away. Let it be there. Check in with it. Anchor in safety, then check back. As you stay anchored in safety and allow the sensation to be there, the intensity of the defensive state often lowers, and polyvagal ladder climbing can happen.
2423670:
This lesson provides a practical walkthrough of how to describe your internal experiences using Yvette's shutdown state as an example.

Yvette's Shutdown Description: Shape: hollow and empty. Size: small, peanut-sized. Location: in her stomach. Color: black. Temperature: cold. Texture: can't identify (and that's okay). Time: always been there, forever. Want: to be left alone. Action: none, it just is. Image: a black hole. Sound: quiet. Memory: being alone as a child.

You Don't Have to Fill Everything In: You don't need an answer for every category. What you can notice, you can describe. Stay grounded in curiosity and continue to witness and feel it.

Practice with Prompts: You're given two image prompts to practice describing using specific domains (color, temperature, texture, taste, size). This is light practice to help you get the basic idea.

Taste is Valid: Some descriptions might seem odd (like taste), but taste comes up often, especially with emotions like shame and disgust. Whatever pops into your mind is the right answer.
2449552:
This lesson asks you to practice describing your own internal experience, either your UDS goal emotion or any tolerable emotion.

Focus on Your UDS Goal Emotion (or Any Tolerable Emotion): After anchoring in your safety state, invite and allow the emotion that brought you here (your UDS goal). Witness it for a moment. If that's too much, choose any tolerable emotion, even a positive one like happiness.

Identify Three Description Domains: Once you're anchored, have invited the emotion, and are witnessing it, try to identify three of the description domains (shape, size, location, color, temperature, texture, time, want, action, image, sound, memory).

Keep It Tolerable: This should not be too deep, triggering, or dysregulating. Keep it tolerable. You're practicing these concepts and bringing them closer to home, but it should not be too much.
2495109: This video guides you through combining the skills of balancing and awe to connect with defensive activation while anchoring in safety. You'll learn how to align your cognitive and bodily experiences to foster self-regulation, deepen your connection with defensive emotions, and build resilience through repeated practice. By focusing on manageable emotions and using the AWE method, you'll enhance your nervous system's capacity to tolerate and regulate challenging states.
2454701:
This is a guided Balancing and A-W-E practice where you'll anchor into safety, invite defensive activation, and balance the two while staying present.

Step 1: Anchor into Safety (Cue to Anchor): Start by validating whatever emotion you're currently feeling. Normalize it ("I feel this way and that makes sense because..."). Give it an image if needed, and invite it to be with you. Then, use your safety cue and mindfully experience it, notice how it feels, its color, shape, temperature, texture, and how it affects your breathing and muscle tension.

Step 2: Identify and Witness Safety: Notice where safety lives in your body. Describe it using the "silly questions" (color, shape, temperature, texture). Spend time with this feeling.

Step 3: Make a Choice: You can stop here and call it a win, or if you have curiosity, you can move on and invite some defensive activation. There is no shame in stopping.

Step 4: Witness Defense (A-W): Identify a defensive experience (either one that's already there or one you want to give focus to). Notice the emotion word that fits it. Ask yourself if it makes sense why you have this experience. Notice where it lives in your body and describe it using the "silly questions."

Step 5: Balance Defense with Safety: Check on your breath. Check on the safety emotion you identified earlier, where is it now? Has it changed? Remind yourself that you're safe.

Step 6: Reconnect with the External World: Open your eyes. Notice what you see in front of you, to the left, to the right. Let your body move if it wants to. Take an intentional breath. Say something nice to yourself.

2495013:
Directions:After completing the practice in #Balancing & A->W->E: Practice (shorter)and/or #Balancing & A->W->E: Practice (longer), reflect or journal on the following. (You do not need to answer all of them.)

  • What was your overall experience of this Skills Practice?

  • How was this emotionally? Did you notice any emotions surface you did not expect? Was it difficult to connect with an emotion?

  • How did this practice affect you cognitively? Did you notice any thoughts surface you did not expect? Was it difficult to focus on the practice?

  • Did anything else unexpected surface?

  • Is this something you can practice again? How much curiosity and motivation do you have to practice again?

  • Does this skill cause you to feel more or less motivation to continue down the Unstucking Pathway?
2495257:
Directions:Lead yourself through the Balancing & AWE skill.

  • If you’re able to permit a defensive emotion and then balance it with safety at the AWE level, you’re ready to move to the next lesson. Or, you could try balancing a more difficult emotion.

  • You should be able to describe what defense feels like and balance it with safety.

  • If you’re unable to complete this on your own, return to the guided version in #Balancing & A->W->E: Guided Meditation from the previous step. Take your time, there is no rush.
2449452:
This lesson introduces Pendulation, the ability to move back and forth between safety and defense while staying anchored.

Pendulation is Balancing Safety and Defense: You want to allow both safety and defense to exist at the same time. Defense is already there, so you give it permission to be present, but you don't let it get out of control. You balance it with your safety state.

The Pendulation Process: 1) Give permission for and stay anchored in your safety state (this is always the priority). 2) Give permission for the discomfort to emerge or remain present. 3) Experience the discomfort mindfully using A-W-E (feel, describe, notice). 4) Allow the discomfort to remain, then pendulate over to and feel your safety state. Repeat.

Benefits of Pendulation: Reduction in immediate discomfort. The two states (safety and defense) may interact and shift, eventually merging into something else. More curiosity for your defensive state. Increased distress tolerance and vagal brake strength.

Uses for Pendulation: For returning or discharging flight/fight energy. For making discomfort tolerable. For building the strength of your vagal brake and safety state.
2423675:
This lesson provides guided Pendulation practice using video prompts to help you notice and move between different emotional reactions.

Notice Your Immediate Reaction: You'll watch a series of video pairs. Notice your immediate reaction to the first video (on the left). Try to hang on to that reaction with curiosity while staying grounded in safety.

Three Key Prompts: After each video, ask yourself: 1) Can you give your experience an emotion name? 2) Can you describe what that emotion was like? 3) How did this video affect your breathing?

Pendulate Between the Two: After watching both videos in a pair, you'll see them together on the screen. Purposefully pendulate back and forth between your two experiences. Notice if the intensity of your reaction softens or shifts.

Keep It Tolerable: These should not be hugely triggering. If they are, stop and do some safety anchoring. Come back when you're ready. This is just practice, you're getting the idea and building the skill.
2423673: This video guides you through a pendulation practice, helping you gently navigate between feelings of defensive activation and safety. You'll learn to validate and normalize your emotions, mindfully explore your safety cues, and develop a deeper connection with your nervous system to enhance self-regulation. By practicing this technique, you'll build resilience and foster a greater sense of calm and presence.
2449451: This video guides you through an advanced pendulation practice to help you safely navigate between defensive activation and a sense of safety. You'll learn to validate and normalize your emotions, mindfully explore physical sensations, and strengthen your ability to self-regulate by anchoring into safety while gently engaging with challenging feelings. This practice enhances your nervous system awareness and builds resilience through intentional, embodied mindfulness.

Directions:Lead yourself through the Pendulation & AWE skill.

2423678:
This lesson introduces Titration, the process of allowing stuck defensive energy to release or return a little bit at a time.

Titration is Releasing Stuck Energy Gradually: Titration means allowing some stuck, defensive, frozen state energy to release at a time, not all at once. This prevents re-traumatization and allows you to come out of immobility or shutdown gradually.

Titration Uses Mindful Experiencing and Pendulation: You must be anchored in your safety state to be mindful. Bring that mindfully anchored safety state to your defensive state, be curious, allow it to be there, feel it. Then pendulate back and forth between safety and defense.

What Titration Feels Like: You might notice shakes, trembles, tingles, waves, shutters, a "staticy" feeling, or fireworks popping. It could also feel like irritability, snappiness, or anger as fight energy returns from shutdown. There's no right or wrong way to experience it.

Always Prioritize Anchoring in Safety: When you notice these things happening, don't beat yourself up. Notice it. Apologize if needed. Prioritize anchoring in safety. Then, if you can, allow yourself to feel the defensive state mindfully and pendulate back to safety.

⏳ Change is Incremental: Titration allows you to build tolerance as you release a little bit, anchor in safety, release a little bit, anchor in safety. This builds the strength of your vagal brake. Don't push yourself further than you're capable of going.
2423679:
This lesson explains the relationship between fear, immobility, and the discharge of stuck flight/fight energy.

Fear is the Experience of Your Stuck State Impulse: Fear and immobility go hand in hand. Fear is experienced when you have flight/fight activation but cannot act on the impulse to run away or fight. If you're immobile while in flight/fight, that's freeze, and the immobility locks in the flight/fight energy, which is experienced as fear.

If You Can Act on the Impulse, Fear is Not Experienced: If you can successfully run away or fight, you'll have an adrenaline rush, but you won't experience fear. Fear is the inability to act on the impulse.

Your Stuck State Discharge Lies Under or Through the Fear: Fear might be an obstacle, but it's also an indicator of progress or your next stuck point. When stuck state impulses, sensations, or energies emerge, fear might come along with it. You need to notice it while grounding yourself in safety, then allow the sensations and impulses of the stuck state.

You Need Vagal Brake Strength to Handle Fear: Normalize the experience of fear. Give yourself permission to have it. It's not because you're weak, it's because there's an impulse that hasn't been completed yet. You need to come at your fear with curiosity, interest, and self-empathy (not judgment) while staying anchored in your safety state.

Feeling Fear is Not a Failure: If you feel fear, notice it. You might need to pause, do some self-regulation, and come back. Fear could be a good sign that you're on the right track, but make sure your vagal brake is strong enough to handle it.
2449561:
This lesson explains what discharge is and how to recognize and allow it to happen.

Discharge is When the Lock of Immobility is Softened: When the lock of immobility is off, your frozen sympathetic energy can release. The impulse to escape or be powerful can surface and even be acted on. Discharge is what happens when you can simply act on the stuck, frozen impulse.

Moments of Discharge Have Varying Experiences: Discharge can look like tingles, waves, surges, shaking, shuttering, trembling, or spontaneous changes in breathing. None of these experiences are chosen, they are biological processes that unfold, which you can witness and experience.

Discharge is Allowed, Not Forced: You don't force discharge. You allow it. You witness it with third-party objectivity (A-W-E method), then delve deeper and directly experience it. It's not a disconnected process, you're very much attuned and experiencing it.

Reference Points for Discharge: Think of when you shudder (like when you're cold or watching a horror movie and shake it off). Or think of orgasm, there's tensing, immobilization, then releasing with waves, trembles, and shaking. The experience is different, but the waves are very similar.

Mindfully Experience the Whole Process: You want to mindfully experience what leads up to discharge (from behavior to emotion, cognition, sensations, and impulses) and then the discharge itself, which will have its own distinct experience.
2423680:
This lesson builds on the previous one by exploring the impulses that arise from each rung of your Polyvagal ladder.

Know What to Expect at Each Rung: It's important to get an idea of what to expect as you access the different rungs of your Polyvagal ladder. You want to know what it feels like and what impulses may arise from that rung.

Impulses are Indicators: If you're feeling certain impulses, it's a pretty good indication of where you're at on your ladder. But don't get too wrapped up in the cognition of "where am I on my ladder?"

Focus on the Experience: Instead of analyzing your position, focus on the experience of the present moment and whatever's coming up inside of you. The goal is to be present with your internal experience, not to intellectually categorize it.
2423681:
This lesson explores the impulses that arise from your safety state, connection, play, and stillness.

Safety Impulses are About Connection: Connection with yourself (internal awareness, self-regulation) and connection with others (eye contact, smiles, listening, empathy, touch, vocal prosody). These impulses just happen when you're in your safety state, your body simply does them.

Play Impulses are About Mobilization and Socialization: Play is the mixed state (safe and social + mobilization). You'll have an impulse to move and an impulse to connect. Play involves movement, co-regulation, spontaneity, imagination, sharing, taking turns, and empathizing.

Stillness Impulses are About Immobilizing and Experiencing the Present Moment: You'll have an impulse to not move. You'll focus on the present moment, take in your sensory experience (internal and external), be more reflective, and breathe. You'll be immobile without fear.

Mindfully Experience These Impulses: Notice the faces and voices of those you're playing with. Notice the movement in your body. Notice your breath and where it naturally goes. Allow your body to breathe the way it wants to breathe. Notice the absence of fear when you're immobile in stillness.
2449583:
This lesson explores the impulses that arise from the flight state and how to work with them.

Flight Impulses are About Escape: The impulse for flight is to escape, to mobilize, and to create space. Flight is about mobilization to get away and reach safety. The word "escape" is key.

Mindfully Experience Flight Energy: You can use flight energy physically (sprinting, jogging, jumping, climbing, dancing) or through imagination (like Peter Levine's example of Nancy escaping from an imaginary tiger). There's no one right way, listen to what your body wants.

Anxiousness May Indicate Flight Energy: If you notice anxiousness, it could be an indicator that you have more flight energy in your system. Instead of getting rid of the anxiety, use A-W-E to experience it. An escape impulse may arise from that.

Avoidance vs. Escape: Avoidance is using a behavior to go around flight activation (like taking an alternate route home). Escape is successfully using your flight activation (like running away from a danger on the way home). Avoidance is where you're avoiding using the energy to get to safety, you're just going around the issue.
2449584:
This lesson explores the impulses that arise from the fight state and how to work with them.

Fight Impulses are About Using Force: Fight impulses are about using mobilization to enclose space, to get closer to the danger, not get away from it. Fight happens when flight hasn't worked. If you can use force and aggression in a closer space, the danger may back off, and then you can escape.

Mindfully Experience Fight Energy: You can use fight energy physically (throwing, hitting, strangling, squeezing, pushing, lifting) or through imagination (telling someone off in your mind). Do NOT use fight impulses on yourself or anybody else. If you want to use it physically, do organized activities like boxing lessons.

Irritability May Indicate Fight Energy: If you notice irritability, anger, snapping at people, talking more firmly, yelling, or blaming, it could be an indicator that you have more fight energy in your system. This is a good time to feel into it and do some unstucking work.

Anger vs. Power: Anger is exerting force and dominance at another person's expense (acting out of selfishness). Power is exerting force along with healthy boundaries and self-respect (acting out of self-interest). Power recognizes that other people can make their own choices, but you're also allowed to push back and say no.
2449585:
This lesson explores the impulses that arise from the shutdown state and how to work with them.

Shutdown Impulses are About Appearing Dead: The impulse is to feign death, to appear dead, to immobilize, to appear non-threatening, and to be invisible. From shutdown, the impulse would be to come out of it, up into fight, then flight, then safety and connection.

Mindfully Experience the Conservation: You probably need to reduce stimulation, listen for quiet, look at calmness, focus on one or two things at a time (small things, maybe right in front of you). Experience the safety of your environment. Work small and expand.

Sadness or Anhedonia May Indicate Shutdown: If you notice more sadness or anhedonia (the inability to experience happiness), it's a good indication that you're in a shutdown state. You might notice a pull toward being alone, sitting down, or laying down. This is a good time to immobilize, go to your safety state, and feel into what you're experiencing.

Isolation vs. Solitude: Isolation is being by yourself, probably with judgment (like locking yourself in your room and telling others to leave you alone). Solitude is immobilizing in safety and welcoming shutdown (like using your safety environment, reducing stimulation, and allowing for immobilization without judgment).
2449586:
This lesson explores the impulses that arise from the freeze state and how to work with them.

Freeze Impulses are About Enduring: Freeze comes down to enduring, surviving, experiencing, bracing for impact, and then exploding in flight or fight energy. It's holding and then releasing. Your body is in a temporary holding state, ready to release.

Slowly Thaw the Immobility: You want to slowly thaw the immobility and allow the flight/fight energy to titrate out a bit at a time through pendulation. First, reduce immobility through safety cues (passive and active). Your body needs to feel safe so you can then feel the stuck flight/fight energy.

Allow Sympathetic Energy to Come Out a Bit at a Time: Once your body feels more safe, allow that sympathetic energy (which is frozen in the system) to come out a bit at a time. Have a plan to pause the process and return to it if necessary. Use titration, pendulate and allow a bit of energy to come out at a time.

Mindfully Experience Your Progress: Notice what's different about the intensity of your freeze state this time versus the last time. See that things are getting better, it's not all at once, but it is a process. Do this for all impulses: notice how things shift over time.
